sentences.text: The upper jaw bone of Sinotyrannus features a uniquely curved upper edge that dips inward, contrasting with the outward curve seen in later tyrannosaurs.
Three preserved back vertebrae possess exceptionally tall bony projections along their tops.

The holotype, which serves as the official specimen for the species, consists of a scattered collection of bones including the front of the skull, three back vertebrae, parts of the hip bone, and several hand bones with a claw.
The hip bones are mostly preserved as impressions left in the rock, with the outer surface of the left hip bone being the most complete part.
The front part of the hip blade is short and broad with a large connection point for the pubic bone, while the rear part is longer and thinner with a triangular connection for the ischial bone.
Large, oval-shaped openings at the front of the skull support its link to the Proceratosauridae family.
Although enough bone is missing to be sure, the animal likely had a large ridge on its nose similar to other members of its family.
Its size challenges the old idea that early tyrannosauroids were small and grew larger only in advanced forms like Tyrannosaurus.
The fossil was found in the Early Cretaceous Jiufotang Formation in Liaoning, China, and includes a single partial skeleton.
The specific name honors the Kazuo district in Liaoning where the remains were discovered.
In 2016, scientists updated the size estimates to a length of 7.5 meters and a weight of 1.2 tons.
Sinotyrannus is classified within the family Proceratosauridae.
Its parent group is Proceratosauridae.
Its family is Proceratosauridae.
The type species is Sinotyrannus kazuoensis.
The original description suggested it might be the oldest tyrannosaur due to its large size, but later analyses place it as a proceratosaurid tyrannosaur.
Conversely, a 2016 analysis placed Juratyrant and Stokesosaurus outside Proceratosauridae and proposed that Sinotyrannus is a sister taxon to Yutyrannus within Proceratosauridae.
Sinotyrannus lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 120 million years ago during the Aptian stage, in what is now Asia.
It inhabited a wet environment characterized by well-watered forests and large lakes.
The environment where Sinotyrannus lived was prone to high levels of volcanism.
Recent research suggests that Sinotyrannus, known from an adult specimen, may be a mature form of the earlier named genus Huaxiagnathus, which is known only from immature specimens.
